en.title: How to Check Whether a Land Deed Is Genuine
en.directAnswer: A deed can look real and still be unsafe. Check the registration record, the seller’s identity, the property description, the chain of earlier deeds, current land records, mutation, tax records and any available mortgage information. A genuine document does not always mean the seller has complete legal title.

atAGlance.whoFor: A buyer wants to reduce the risk of a fake or misleading deed.
atAGlance.legalBasis: Registration Act, 1908; Transfer of Property Act, 1882; official Registration Directorate and land records.
atAGlance.mainRule: Verification should compare the document with official records, not only the paper shown by the seller.
atAGlance.updateStatus: Re-check any new Registration Directorate digital verification service before publication.

en.lawMeaning: Verification should compare the document with official records, not only the paper shown by the seller. This page gives a general route. A person’s exact rights can change because of facts, documents, deadlines, legal status, court orders or later amendments.
steps: Match deed number, date and registration office.
Compare property description with khatian and map.
Ask why any record does not match.
evidence: Original deed; certified copy where available; NID; earlier deeds; khatian; mutation; map; tax receipts; mortgage information.
en.simpleExample: A seller shows a clean-looking deed, but the plot number in the deed does not match the latest land record. That mismatch should be resolved before purchase.
commonMistakes: Common mistakes: Checking only the stamp paper.
Common mistakes: trusting a scanned copy.
Common mistakes: not checking seller identity.
Common mistakes: assuming registration means no mortgage exists..
